title: Voluntary and reflex actions compared
content:
Not everything the nervous system does is automatic. A voluntary action is one you decide to make: reaching for a book, speaking, or stepping around a puddle. The stimulus may still start the process — you see the puddle — but the decision is made consciously in the brain, and only then are instructions sent down motor neurones to your muscles.

The table shows the important differences.

FeatureReflex actionVoluntary action
Decision made inspinal cord (not the conscious brain)the conscious brain
Speedvery rapidslower
Automatic?yes — cannot easily be preventedno — you choose to do it
Exampleblinking when something moves towards the eyeraising your hand to answer a question

Why the body needs both kinds

Reflexes are essential for protection, but they are crude — they always give the same response to the same stimulus. Voluntary actions are slower, but they can be varied, planned and learned. A pianist’s fingers make voluntary actions, chosen and ordered by the brain; if a wasp lands on their neck, the flinching reflex takes over without waiting for the brain to vote on it. The two systems work alongside each other all day.

A common misconception: reflexes are not “just fast voluntary actions”. The difference is not only speed but where the decision is processed. If the conscious brain is involved in choosing the response, it is a voluntary action, however quick.

Practice

Classify each of these as a reflex or a voluntary action, giving a reason: (a) salivating when you smell food; (b) walking to the kitchen; (c) sneezing when dust enters your nose.

Show the answer

(a) Reflex — the stimulus (the smell) produces an automatic response that you cannot simply decide not to make. (b) Voluntary — you choose to start, stop and steer the walking; the brain plans and controls the movement. (c) Reflex — the sneeze is produced automatically by the reflex arc in response to the dust stimulus, without any conscious decision.

title: The eye: structure
content:
The eye is a sense organ: its receptors detect light and convert it into nerve messages. To understand its two reflex responses — changing the pupil and focusing — you first need to know the parts of the eye and what each one does.

Parts and their jobs

  • The sclera is the tough outer coat (the visible “white” of the eye at the front), which protects the eyeball.
  • The cornea is the transparent window at the front. It begins focusing the light.
  • The iris is the coloured part. Its muscles change the size of the pupil.
  • The pupil is the gap in the middle of the iris — the hole that light passes through.
  • The lens changes shape to focus light precisely onto the retina.
  • The ciliary muscles and suspensory ligaments work together to change the shape of the lens.
  • The retina lines the back of the eye and contains light-sensitive receptor cells.
  • The optic nerve carries impulses from the retina to the brain.

Two refracting parts, one job

Focusing light is shared between two structures. The cornea, fixed and curved, bends the light first; the lens, adjustable, fine-focuses it. The lens is the part that can be altered, which is why everything about focusing (page 9) is about changing the lens — never about moving the whole eye closer or further from its own retina.

Practice

Match each part with the correct job: retina, iris, optic nerve, lens. The jobs: carries impulses to the brain; contains light receptors; changes shape to focus light; changes the size of the pupil.

Show the answer

The optic nerve carries impulses from the retina to the brain; the retina contains the light-sensitive receptor cells; the lens changes shape to focus light precisely onto the retina; the iris changes the size of the pupil, adjusting how much light enters the eye.

title: The pupil reflex
content:
The pupil looks like a black spot in the middle of the iris, but it is not a solid object — it is simply the gap through which light enters the inside of the eye. Because it is a gap controlled by muscles, its size can change. This is the pupil reflex.

The reflex arc, applied to the eye

The pupil reflex follows exactly the chain from page 1:

  • stimulus: the light level on the eye changes (brighter or dimmer);
  • receptors: light-sensitive cells in the retina detect the change;
  • co-ordinator: the message passes along the optic nerve to the brain, which sends instructions back;
  • effector: the muscles of the iris;
  • response: the pupil becomes smaller or wider.

Notice a difference from the spinal reflex on page 5: this reflex is co-ordinated by the brain, but still automatically — the unconscious part of the brain, not the conscious part. You cannot stop your pupil from shrinking in bright light by deciding to.

Why the reflex exists

In very bright light, too much light would damage the light-sensitive cells of the retina, so the pupil shrinks to limit the light entering. In dim light, too little light would make seeing impossible, so the pupil widens to let more in. The reflex keeps the amount of light inside the eye in a working range — the same principle of keeping conditions controlled that you will meet again with blood glucose on page 12.

Practice

A person walks out of a dark cinema into bright afternoon daylight. Describe what happens to their pupils, and explain why this response is a reflex.

Show the answer

The bright daylight is the stimulus; receptors in the retina detect it, and instructions from the brain cause the muscles of the iris to contract so that the pupils become smaller, letting less light into the eye and protecting the retina from damage. It is a reflex because it is automatic and rapid — it happens without the person deciding on it, and cannot be prevented by choice.

title: Accommodation: focusing near and far
content:
The cornea and the lens together must focus light into a sharp image exactly on the retina — not in front of it, not behind it. Objects at different distances send light to the eye in different ways: light from a distant object arrives as almost parallel rays, while light from a near object spreads out (diverges) more. One fixed lens could not focus both sharply. The eye solves this by changing the shape of the lens, a process called accommodation.

The mechanism, step by step

The lens sits in a ring of ciliary muscles, attached to the lens by the suspensory ligaments. The two states work like this:

  • Distant object: the ciliary muscles relax, which pulls the ring outwards. The suspensory ligaments are drawn tight and tug the lens into a thin shape. A thin lens bends the light less — right for nearly parallel rays.
  • Near object: the ciliary muscles contract, pulling the ring inwards. The suspensory ligaments go slack, and the lens springs back into a fatter, rounder shape. A fat lens bends the light more — right for diverging rays.

A useful memory rule: the lens has to work harder for near objects, and the muscle also works harder — contracting — for near objects.

A common misconception: the lens does not slide backwards and forwards to focus (that is how a camera focuses). The lens stays in exactly the same place — only its shape changes, from thin to fat and back.

Practice

Describe what the ciliary muscles and the suspensory ligaments are doing while you read this page, compared with when you look up at the far wall.

Show the answer

Reading is near work: the ciliary muscles are contracted and the suspensory ligaments are slack, so the lens is fat and bends the diverging light enough to focus it on the retina. Looking at the far wall, the ciliary muscles relax, the suspensory ligaments tighten and stretch the lens thin, bending the almost-parallel light less.

title: Comparing nervous and hormonal control
content:
So far this chapter has followed the nervous system. The body’s second control system sends its messages differently. Hormones are chemicals released into the blood by glands. Because they travel in the bloodstream, they reach everywhere the blood reaches — but they are carried at the speed of circulating blood, far slower than a nerve impulse, and they are diluted by the blood as they go.

The table compares the two systems.

FeatureNervous systemHormonal system
Message carrierelectrical impulses along neuroneshormones in the blood
Speedvery fastslower
How long the effect lastsshort — the response stops when the impulses stoplonger — until the hormone is broken down
Where the message goesalong specific nerves to specific cellsall around the body, but affects only its target organs

Why the body needs both

Each system suits a different kind of job. Escaping danger needs split-second timing, so it is handled by nerves: impulses sprint from your eyes to your spinal cord to your leg muscles. Growth, by contrast, must be steady over years — no use for a message that switches off after a millisecond — so growth is controlled by hormones. In this chapter’s own example, the pupil reflex uses nerves because the amount of light entering the eye must be corrected at once, while the control of glucose in your blood uses the hormone insulin because glucose is arriving steadily for hours after a meal.

The key idea: fast, brief, precisely targeted jobs go to nerves; slower, longer-lasting, whole-body jobs go to hormones. Both systems still follow the same chain from page 1 — stimulus, receptor, co-ordinator, effector, response.

Practice

For each situation, state which system you would expect to control it, and justify your choice: (a) your hand pulling back from a thorn; (b) the steady growth of a child over several years.

Show the answer

(a) Nervous — the response must be extremely fast and brief, and must go to the specific muscles of the arm, which is exactly what nerve impulses along the reflex arc achieve. (b) Hormonal — growth is a slow, long-lasting process affecting the whole body over years, which suits chemical messages carried in the blood over long periods.
